title: Sampling, Regression and Correlation
lines: This topic links samples to populations and one variable to another. USAT asks you to name sampling methods, count possible samples, use the standard error, build a confidence interval, read the vocabulary of hypothesis testing, fit and use a regression line, interpret the correlation coefficient and recognise the components of a time series.
## Population and sample
- A parameter describes a population (μ, σ) and is fixed; a statistic describes a sample (x̄, s) and varies from sample to sample.

- Probability methods: simple random (equal chance for every unit), stratified (random sample from each homogeneous group), systematic (every kth unit after a random start, k = N ÷ n), cluster (whole groups chosen at random).
- Non-probability methods include convenience, judgement and quota sampling.
- Sampling error = statistic − parameter. It falls as n grows; it is not a recording mistake.
- Number of possible samples of size n from N units: Nⁿ with replacement (order counted), ᴺCₙ without replacement.
## Sampling distribution of the mean
- Mean of all possible x̄ values = μ, so x̄ is unbiased for μ.
- Standard error: σ_x̄ = σ ÷ √n with replacement (or for a large population).
- Central limit theorem: for large n (usually 30 or more), x̄ is approximately normal whatever the population shape.
> Example 1. σ = 12, n = 36. SE = 12 ÷ 6 = 2. To halve SE, multiply n by 4.
## Estimation
A point estimate is one number, such as x̄ for μ. An interval estimate gives a range: x̄ ± z·σ/√n.
| Confidence | z
For a proportion, SE = √(p̂q̂ ÷ n).
> Example 2. n = 100, x̄ = 50, σ = 10. SE = 1, so the 95 % interval is 50 ± 1.96 = 48.04 to 51.96.
## Hypothesis testing basics
- H₀ is the null hypothesis of no difference; H₁ is the alternative.
- Type I error: rejecting a true H₀, with probability α (the level of significance). Type II error: accepting a false H₀, with probability β.
- H₁: μ ≠ μ₀ gives a two-tailed test; H₁: μ > μ₀ or μ < μ₀ gives a one-tailed test.
- z = (x̄ − μ₀) ÷ (σ/√n). At 5 %, reject H₀ if |z| > 1.96 (two-tailed) or z > 1.645 (right-tailed).
! Divide by the standard error σ/√n, not by σ. This slip shrinks z and leads to the wrong decision.
## Regression
The regression line of y on x, ŷ = a + bx, is fitted by least squares: it makes Σ(y − ŷ)² as small as possible.
- b = [nΣxy − ΣxΣy] ÷ [nΣx² − (Σx)²], and a = ȳ − b·x̄, so the line passes through (x̄, ȳ).
- b is the change in y for a one-unit rise in x. Use y on x to predict y; use the separate line x on y to predict x.
## Correlation
- r = Σ(x − x̄)(y − ȳ) ÷ √[Σ(x − x̄)² Σ(y − ȳ)²], with −1 ≤ r ≤ +1.
- r = ±1: points on a straight line; r = 0: no linear relation (a curve may still exist).
- r² = b_yx × b_xy, and r has the same sign as both regression coefficients.
- r is unchanged by adding constants or multiplying by positive numbers.
- Spearman's rank correlation: ρ = 1 − 6Σd² ÷ [n(n² − 1)].
> Example 4. b_yx = 0.8, b_xy = 0.45. r² = 0.36, so r = 0.6.
! Correlation is not causation. A third factor, such as hot weather, can drive two variables together.
## Time series
| Component | Example
| Secular trend | population growth over decades
| Seasonal variation | sweet sales before Eid each year
| Cyclical variation | boom and recession over several years
| Irregular variation | a sudden flood
Trend can be found by semi-averages, moving averages or a least squares line y = a + bt. A 3-year moving average of 10, 14, 12, 16 gives 12 and 14.
## Quick check
- N = 6, n = 2 without replacement: how many samples?
- What is the 99 % z value?
- If b_yx = −0.5 and b_xy = −0.32, find r.
- Which time series component repeats every year?
